mappings.note: Reactant/product terminology. Equation vocabulary sits under C 1.3's competency text; C 1.3-LO-1 is specifically about writing a BALANCED equation with states, which is not what is asked.
Explicitly asks for the UNBALANCED formula representation, so C 1.3-LO-1 (balanced equation) is excluded by the stem itself; the competency covers representing a reaction with symbols.
Why symbolic representation beats words -- a question about the value of the notation, not about balancing, so the competency and not C 1.3-LO-1.
Bare formula recall (H2O). No equation, so competency level, consistent with the other formula items in this chapter.
Defines a skeletal equation, which by definition is the unbalanced form; C 1.3-LO-1 would contradict the stem.

Sits inside the skeletal-equation cluster (qid:700193, qid:700195) and the given Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2 is left deliberately unbalanced, so the expected answer is 'skeletal/unbalanced equation'. Flagged as ambiguous: if the intended answer were 'displacement reaction' it would belong at C 1.2-LO-1, but the option text is not stored.
Asks WHY a skeletal equation must be balanced -- the conservation-of-mass justification, which is LO-2 and not the balancing procedure of LO-1.
Statement of the law of conservation of mass itself, the concept LO-2 is built on.
Why atom counts must match on both sides -- conservation of mass reasoning, LO-2 rather than the mechanics of balancing.
10 g + 5 g gives 15 g of products: a numerical application of conservation of mass. LO-2 rather than LO-1 because no equation is written.
Which formula to balance first is part of the procedure for producing a balanced equation, so LO-1. Not LO-2: no justification for balancing is asked.
Applies the 'most atoms first' rule to Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2 -- balancing technique under LO-1.
Rationale for the 'most atoms first' heuristic. Still balancing procedure, so LO-1; the conservation argument of LO-2 is not what is probed.
Defines the hit-and-trial balancing method -- the skill LO-1 names.
The rule that subscripts must not be altered while balancing is a constraint on how a balanced equation is produced, so LO-1 rather than LO-2.
Where coefficients go when balancing -- balancing mechanics, LO-1.

Meaning of (aq). This is the 'states the physical states of the reactants and products' half of C 1.3-LO-1. C 8.1-LO-1 rejected because its named symbols are precipitate, gas and heat, and (aq) is none of those.
Which symbol marks a gaseous substance. C 8.1-LO-1 names the gas symbol explicitly, so it is a closer fit than C 1.3-LO-1's general physical-states clause.
Meaning of (s) as the solid state. Kept at C 1.3-LO-1 rather than C 8.1-LO-1 because the stem asks about the state symbol generally, not about reading (s) as a precipitate.
Where reaction conditions such as heat or a catalyst are written in an equation -- interpreting the notation above the arrow, which C 8.1-LO-1 covers via the heat symbol.
The delta above the arrow means heat is required -- the heat symbol named verbatim in C 8.1-LO-1.
Reading MnO2 above the arrow as a catalyst. Catalyst is not in C 8.1-LO-1's named list, but interpreting a symbol written over the arrow is squarely that outcome and no other code comes closer.
Definition-to-name of a combination reaction, the first type LO-1 lists.
Picks a combination reaction from examples -- LO-1 classification.
Classifies 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O as a combination reaction. The equation is given already balanced, so C 1.3-LO-1 does not apply.
Names the class of reaction that releases heat (exothermic). Energy classification has no learning outcome in this frame, so competency level, as throughout this chapter.
Example of an exothermic reaction -- same frame gap as qid:700214.
What happens to temperature during an exothermic reaction. Energy change, no LO available.
Definition-to-name of a decomposition reaction, named in LO-1.
Picks the decomposition reaction from examples -- LO-1 classification.
Why decompositions need an energy input. The point tested is the endothermic character rather than recognising a decomposition, and energy has no LO here, so competency level.
Names thermal decomposition -- a sub-type of the decomposition category in LO-1.
Classifies CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 on heating as thermal decomposition -- LO-1.
Which observation is typical of FeSO4 thermal decomposition: identifying a decomposition from what is seen and smelt, LO-1 word for word.
Names photolytic decomposition -- still the decomposition clause of LO-1.
Classifies 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2 in sunlight as photolytic decomposition, LO-1.
The greying of AgCl in photography attributed to photolytic decomposition. LO-1, not LO-2 -- nothing here is corrosion, despite the stored tag.
Names the class of reaction that absorbs energy (endothermic) -- the energy-change gap, competency level.
Example of an endothermic process -- same gap as qid:700226.
How the test tube feels during an endothermic reaction. Energy observation, no LO available.
Definition-to-name of a displacement reaction, named in LO-1.
Classifies Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu as displacement -- LO-1, the equation being supplied.
Why zinc displaces copper: the reactivity reasoning behind the displacement clause of LO-1.
Names a precipitation reaction from its definition -- the double displacement/precipitation clause of LO-1.
Classifies Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + NaCl as double displacement/precipitation. Classification only, so not C 1.3-LO-1.
The term 'precipitate' for the insoluble product. C 8.1-LO-1 rejected: the question asks for the word, not for the (s) symbol that denotes it.
Defines oxidation by gain of oxygen / loss of hydrogen -- the oxidation clause of LO-1.
Copper blackening in air classified as oxidation -- an oxidation identified from an observation, LO-1. Not LO-2: this is a laboratory heating, not an everyday corrosion effect.
Which substance is oxidised in 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO -- redox identification under LO-1.
Defines reduction by loss of oxygen / gain of hydrogen -- the reduction clause of LO-1.
Which substance is reduced in CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O -- LO-1 redox identification.
Best description of a reduction reaction -- LO-1's reduction clause, definitional form.
Names a redox reaction from the simultaneity of oxidation and reduction, both named in LO-1.
Identifies both halves of the redox change in CuO + H2 -- LO-1.
Why the reaction is redox rather than only oxidation or only reduction -- reasoning within LO-1's oxidation and reduction clause.
Names corrosion from its definition -- LO-2's corrosion-of-metals clause.
Picks an example of corrosion. LO-2 rather than LO-1, because the category being tested is the everyday effect of oxidation, not a reaction type.
